# the contributor audit: three fibers with a symmetric middle


`candidate b13e43ee6ee1d8af`.
The subsequently appended all-dimensional cone sharpness is audited below.

The bodies are full dimensional, the bases are exactly -1,0,1, and the
single chosen point is either the middle symmetry center or the centroid
of the larger endpoint. Their membership and convex compatibility are
explicit. No lattice rounding occurs.

For a nonzero continuous normal, reversed closed endpoint caps have zero
boundary volume and their midpoint is in the missed middle half. The
proof invokes Brunn--Minkowski only under P<a, when both residual volumes
are strictly positive. At fixed P the concave root sum has its minimum
at an endpoint; the decreasing-in-base root increment proves that the
smaller endpoint should lose the entire captured mass. This gives the
claimed residual lower bound in all zero and saturated statuses. Pure
integer normals retain the whole middle fiber and at least one endpoint;
their lower bound is no smaller. Passing from a through-point cap to any
containing cap is monotone.

For the scalar minimization, the breakpoint a0=Gamma-h+t is in [0,1]
when h<=Gamma. The quotient decreases to that breakpoint and increases
after it. When Gamma<=h<=1, it instead has its minimum at a=t. The
inverse relation h=2^(-d)(1+t^(1/d))^d is concave as a nonnegative sum of
concave powers; its endpoint comparison with the displayed affine
function proves the desired ratio. The h>=1 case uses a<=1. Every
division has a positive denominator. The binomial identity proves
2 Gamma+rho<=1, with equality exactly in dimensions one and two.
Thus beta=Gamma/(1+2 Gamma+rho)>=Gamma/2, strictly in dimensions at
least three. The calculation also proves the exact scalar minimum.

The planar selector sharpness example has middle area 8/9, endpoint areas
1/9 and 1, and total area 2. The downward middle cap and the finitely
tilted endpoint apex cap both have raw area 4/9. They certify sharpness
only for the specified two candidates, as the source correctly states.

For the all-dimensional extension, let B be the volume-one cone over a
centrally symmetric base at height zero with apex height one. If r=d/(d+1)
and t=(d-1)/(d+1), then (tB+B)/2=rB. The symmetric hull of rB has sections
(r-|z|)D for |z|<=r, after choosing the same base origin, and is exactly
the convex union rB union(-rB). Its volume is therefore 2 r^d=2 Gamma.
The endpoint centroid has height 1/(d+1), by direct integration of
(1-z)^(d-1). Its apex cap has volume r^d=Gamma. Integer tilt one excludes
both other fibers while retaining that endpoint trace. The downward cap
at the middle center also has volume Gamma and zero endpoint volume.
This proves exact selector sharpness beta in every d>=2. It does not
claim that the two-candidate maximum is the global depth of the example.

This closes the stated symmetric-middle, three-positive-fiber class only.
It does not settle arbitrary fiber counts, arbitrary middle bodies,
intrinsic lower-dimensional intersections, or full OC.

## Subsequent Sections 7--8: full audit PASS

The ordinary-depth extension retains an actual point c in K with depth
at least sigma. Its missed halfspace mass is at most (1-sigma)k, so the
monotone residual bound applies without symmetry. The three scalar ranges
h<=H, H<=h<=1, and h>=1 cover the full domain. In the first range the
breakpoint Gamma-rh+t is nonnegative and at most H<=1. In the second,
the minimum over a is at a=t; the concave inverse v(t) is compared with
the correct line through its endpoint at T. The needed endpoint inequality
2H<=1+T follows from convexity of x^d. The same inequality proves the
h>=1 comparison. The claimed beta_d(sigma) is therefore the exact minimum
of the stated scalar certificate. Its sigma threshold is not asserted
to characterize actual extremal bodies.

The deepest ordinary point exists by upper semicontinuity on compact K,
and the maximizing set is compact, permitting the stated deterministic
coordinate selection. The planar example's residual branch and strict
inequality are correctly certified by the two displayed integer square
comparisons. Its separate good-point lower bound uses the actual affine
alignment of the three centroids, so no certificate failure is mistaken
for a depth counterexample.

In Section 8 I checked the two threshold formulas, their agreement at
a=1/9, all three displayed sigma identities, k_u=D/28, and the endpoint
gap factorization. The residual square is at most a throughout the hard
interval, so deleting its outer positive part there is legitimate. The
function (2sqrt(h)-1)_+^2 is globally convex, including the derivative-zero
transition at h=1/4; hence the gap from the affine target is concave.
The lower-endpoint factorization yields h_l<=4/9. On [1/4,4/9], the
factorization (2/3-sqrt(h))(5sqrt(h)-2/3) proves the asserted endpoint
payment. The zero-residual and collapsed-interval cases are separately
covered. This establishes the threshold for every positive middle area.

The necessity statement is explicitly for these two lower certificates.
Above a=1/9 the fixed upper endpoint loses both available payments as
sigma decreases. Below that ratio, a nearby middle area above 1-a does
the same, with the printed residual-zero factorization ensuring the
status. These scalar areas exceed the whole-body Brunn--Minkowski minimum:
for the upper endpoint k_u-v=(10+4x+10x^2)/28>0; for x<=1/3,
1-x^2-v=(3-2x-5x^2)/4>0. No claim of an actual body attaining every scalar
configuration is used. The new planar asymmetric-middle window is proved,
while the general directional center problem remains unproved.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
